title: Spaghetti Carbonara
subtitle: Roman pasta with egg, Pecorino, and guanciale
excerpt: The authentic Roman carbonara: guanciale or pancetta, eggs and yolks, Pecorino Romano, and lots of black pepper. No cream. The heat of the pasta alone sets the sauce. Rich, silky, and ready in 20 minutes.

recipe.sourceNotes: Carbonara is a Roman pasta dish that appeared in Roman cookbooks in the early 1950s, likely created by or for American soldiers stationed in Rome who combined their rations of bacon and egg powder with local pasta. The authentic Roman version uses guanciale (cured pork cheek), Pecorino Romano, eggs and yolks, and no cream whatsoever. The UK version with pancetta is an acceptable substitution. The sauce is emulsified by the starch in the pasta water and the residual heat of the pan: the temperature must be controlled precisely or the eggs scramble.

content.text: Reserve a large mug of the pasta cooking water before draining: this starchy water is the key to the sauce. Take the frying pan off the heat before adding the egg mixture and toss constantly: the residual heat should set the sauce without scrambling the eggs. If it looks too thick, add more pasta water. No cream is needed or appropriate.

items.preparation: finely grated, plus more to serve

content.text: Whisk together the eggs, egg yolks, Pecorino, Parmesan, and black pepper in a bowl. Set aside.
Cook the spaghetti in heavily salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve 400 ml of pasta cooking water. Drain.
Fry the pancetta or guanciale in a large frying pan over medium heat until the fat has rendered and the meat is golden. Remove from the heat.

Add the drained pasta to the pan with the pancetta. Add 100 ml of pasta water. Working quickly off the heat, pour in the egg mixture. Toss constantly, adding more pasta water a splash at a time, until the sauce is silky and coats the pasta. Serve immediately with extra Pecorino.
